newsitem.title: GUAM: Typhoon hampers search for KAL crash victims.
newsitem.headline: Typhoon hampers search for KAL crash victims.

text.p: Searchers failed to find any more bodies on Tuesday after heavy rains washed away roads leading to the wreckage of a crashed Korean Air Lines jet, officials said.

They said investigators were winding down their work at the crash site but investigation would continue for the next several months in a laboratory in Washington where some evidence from the scene had been taken.

"The investigation has not ended. It will not end for many, many months and the answer to the question 'why' will be found," Matthew Furman, family affairs officer of the U.S. National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said.
Investigators might return to Guam to inspect the wreckage again, Furman told a briefing for reporters and relatives of crash victims.
KAL jet flight 801, with 254 aboard, slammed into a hillside jungle three miles (five km) from the pacific island's international airport on Wednesday.
At least 28 people survived, including three Americans, one Japanese and a New Zealander. The rest were South Koreans, KAL said.
Recovery teams struggled to clear the wreckage amid strong winds and rains induced by Typhoon Winnie which grazed the nearby Northern Marianas island on Tuesday.
"The weather has affected the recovery efforts greatly," Furman said. "The roads that were built by the (U.S.) Navy engineers for the past several days have been washed away."
"Despite all of that, some attempt was made today to remove the wreckage. Unfortunately no more bodies were found."
Furman said he expected more success in recovery efforts once the weather improved.
He said 46 of the more than 150 bodies recovered had been identified.
Furman said family members need not stay on Guam to wait for identification of the other bodies.
"As soon as a family member is identified, even if you are in South Korea you will be told immediately," he added.
Clifford Guzman, special assistant to the governor of Guam, said 12 bodies would be airlifted to South Korea on Wednesday and expressed hope more bodies would be recovered as quickly as possible.
But the identification process might slow down, he said.
"We have close to 150 people working on identification....But the process may slow down in the next couple of days because of the difficulties in identifying the bodies."
Furman said that as investigation was being moved to Washington, "we are not likely to have any new facts in the next couple of days. This will be our last investigation briefing."
